messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: rstan request
parts:
Hi, this has come up before, I think… when running Stan from R, I’d like it, by default, to pull in the data from objects of the same name in the R workspace. That way I don’t have to include data(y=y,X=X,N=N) etc in my stan call. Or maybe this feature already exists and I don’t realize it?
Thanks!
A

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: rstan request
parts:
stan(..., data = .GlobalEnv) should already work if y, X, N etc. are all in the global environment. The problem is if you have additional objects in the global environment that stan() can't process. Then I think it throws an error.

Ben

On Tuesday, December 9, 2014 9:21:52 AM UTC-5, Andrew Gelman wrote:

Thanks!
A

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: rstan request
parts:
I'm not keen on what Andrew wants, which I believe is something
that has no "data = ..." argument and just looks in the global
environment by default. Globals are error prone due to the possibility
of accidentally overwriting them (e.g., by downloading some other
package).

But if Ben and Jiqiang think it's OK to do, we could potentially
wait until the model is compiled, then read the variables off
that, then use them as the equivalent of

data = c("y", "X", "N", ...)

to create the var_context used to read in data.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: rstan request
parts:
I share Bob's hesitation about working with globals. But it's worth noting that R is meant to be interactive, with the intent that users work with globals. So Andrew's request finds comfort from the design doc for the R Environment.

It has taken me years to get over my resistance to using global variables in R. One way to think about R is that everything about it that is annoying to "real" programmers makes it more useful for the majority of users.

messages.author: f53f4ca2c430170d
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: rstan request
parts:
How about a function with a short-and-sweet name that you could throw around your data expression, se something like data=f(a,b,z,q), that would pick put the correct things from a given environment. 

It could be implemented as:

 f <- function(..., e=.GlobalEnv) { x <- all.names(substitute(list(...))); x <- x[2:length(x)]; o<-lapply(x, get); names(o) <- x; return(o) }
a <- 5
b <- 3
f(a, b, letters)

you should be able to do: stan(..., data=f(a, b))

That way the Stan call would name the required object without having to say from where (global by default) and it would avoid having to name the same thing twice (  list(a=a, b=b)   ).  All we need is a nice short memorable name.  It's even useful if you want to use another environment, but I usually just do:

with(data, stan(.....)) which makes it clear and short.

Krzysztof

I think it's at least three different things, because if
you change the name of the data variables in the Stan program,
then you are also going to have to

3. (Re)assign the variables in the global environment.

So if you decide in the Stan program to rename a data variable sigma_mu
instead of just sigma, then you'd have to do the following in the global
environment:

> sigma_mu <- sigma;

Punctuation is of course optional

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] rstan request
parts:
Just by analogy, if I want to add two numbers in R, I can do the following:

c <- a + b

I don’t have to do this:
c <- plus(data=c(“a”,”b”))
or
c <- plus(data=list(a=a,b=b))

Similarly, in Stan I just want to fit the damn model. If my Stan program used data x,y,z,n, I’d like R do to the following, for each variable:
- If I directly supply it in the Stan call, use it.
- If I don’t supply it, pull it from my R session.
- If I don’t supply it in my R function, return an error.
If you think it would be a good idea, the R call could print a statement letting the user know which variables were being pulled in from the R session, so that it wouldn’t happen to users without them realizing it.

A

parts:
On Wednesday, December 10, 2014 4:28:13 PM UTC-5, Andrew Gelman wrote:
Just by analogy, if I want to add two numbers in R, I can do the following:

c <- a + b

I don’t have to do this:
c <- plus(data=c(“a”,”b”))
or
c <- plus(data=list(a=a,b=b))

By your analogy, you would also want

x <- rnorm(100)
mean()

to work because the first argument to the mean function is x and an object called x exists in the global environment. Your preferred behavior relies on the fact that the declared names of the variables in the data block of the Stan program are the same as their symbol names in R and that you are calling stan() from the global environment instead of calling stan() from another function. Subtle errors and undefined behavior can crop up otherwise.

R only behaves the way you want when you utilize an environment, as in

lm(y ~ x1 + x2, data = dataset)
with(dataset, lm(y ~ x1 + x2))
do.call(lm, args = list(formula = y ~ x1 + x2), envir = .GlobalEnv)

Similarly, Stan would behave the way you want it to if you just called

stan(file, data = .GlobalEnv)
stan(file, data = dataset)

except that you if the data argument includes any objects that Stan cannot handle, then an error is thrown currently. We could possibly not throw that error if the object does not correspond to any variable declared in the data block of a Stan program.

Ben

Similarly, in Stan I just want to fit the damn model.  If my Stan program used data x,y,z,n, I’d like R do to the following, for each variable:
- If I directly supply it in the Stan call, use it.
- If I don’t supply it, pull it from my R session.
- If I don’t supply it in my R function, return an error.
If you think it would be a good idea, the R call could print a statement letting the user know which variables were being pulled in from the R session, so that it wouldn’t happen to users without them realizing it.

A

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] rstan request
parts:
If we do this (which I'll go on record as objecting to because of
its lack of transparency and its dependence on globals), then we
shouldn't leave it the way it is now where it will pull everything
out of the blog environment into a var_context --- it's going to
make all the behavior depend not only on the relevant global vars,
but also irrelevant ones.

Let's try to at least remain as modular as possible.

So what I'd propose (if we do this) is to add a new code-generated
method to the generated model class

std::vector<std::string> data_variable_names();

that returns a vector of data variable names. This should only take
me a day or so, including testing.

Then, we would create a var_context from the model and an environment
(defaulting to the global environment) that would pull out all the
variables named in the model from the global environment to create
a var_context.

My main objection to all of this is that it's not clear from the call
stan(...) which dependencies there are on the global environment. You
need to look inside the file/string defining the Stan model for that.

I can also anticipate Andrew's next request, which will be to pull out of the
list just the variables given by the list, and pull the rest out of the
global environment, but maybe we should punt on that (though the
stacking/chainging/whatevering var_context should allow it pretty easily).

- Bob

As Ben pointed out, this is some data preprocessing in stan().  So even you can pass .GlobalEnv, it might not be a good idea to do it.  In particular, it needs to check if doubles can be converted to integers without losing precision.

Jiqiang

On Wed, Dec 10, 2014 at 4:58 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:
It always has worked (unless you have an object lurking in .GlobalEnv or dataset that stan() can't process, in which case it does not work).


On Wednesday, December 10, 2014 4:57:22 PM UTC-5, Andrew Gelman wrote:
Doing stan(file, data = .GlobalEnv) or stan(file, data = dataset), that would work.
A

On Dec 10, 2014, at 4:55 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:

On Wednesday, December 10, 2014 4:28:13 PM UTC-5, Andrew Gelman wrote:
Just by analogy, if I want to add two numbers in R, I can do the following: 

c <- a + b 

I don’t have to do this: 
c <- plus(data=c(“a”,”b”)) 
or 
c <- plus(data=list(a=a,b=b)) 

By your analogy, you would also want

x <- rnorm(100)
mean()

to work because the first argument to the mean function is x and an object called x exists in the global environment. Your preferred behavior relies on the fact that the declared names of the variables in the data block of the Stan program are the same as their symbol names in R and that you are calling stan() from the global environment instead of calling stan() from another function. Subtle errors and undefined behavior can crop up otherwise.

R only behaves the way you want when you utilize an environment, as in

lm(y ~ x1 + x2, data = dataset)
with(dataset, lm(y ~ x1 + x2))
do.call(lm, args = list(formula = y ~ x1 + x2), envir = .GlobalEnv)

Similarly, Stan would behave the way you want it to if you just called

stan(file, data = .GlobalEnv)
stan(file, data = dataset)

except that you if the data argument includes any objects that Stan cannot handle, then an error is thrown currently. We could possibly not throw that error if the object does not correspond to any variable declared in the data block of a Stan program.

Ben
 

Similarly, in Stan I just want to fit the damn model.  If my Stan program used data x,y,z,n, I’d like R do to the following, for each variable: 
- If I directly supply it in the Stan call, use it. 
- If I don’t supply it, pull it from my R session. 
- If I don’t supply it in my R function, return an error. 
If you think it would be a good idea, the R call could print a statement letting the user know which variables were being pulled in from the R session, so that it wouldn’t happen to users without them realizing it. 

A

On Wed, Dec 10, 2014 at 5:20 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
If we do this (which I'll go on record as objecting to because of
its lack of transparency and its dependence on globals), then we
shouldn't leave it the way it is now where it will pull everything
out of the blog environment into a var_context --- it's going to
make all the behavior depend not only on the relevant global vars,
but also irrelevant ones.

I agree with Bob.  I don't like the idea of looking for objects in an environment without being told. 

Jiqiang
